title: No Single Model Fits All: Conflict Decision-Making Models Vary More Across Datasets Than Across Tasks
description: Conflict variants of evidence accumulation models are widely used to explain human cognitive control. However, the generalizability of these models is largely unknown because of the lack of systematic comparisons across multiple conflict tasks and multiple datasets. Here, using a unified amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) framework, we compare the standard DDM and three conflict-specific variants across a benchmark database comprising eight independent studies (N = 1,375). We validate the ABI as a common framework for model comparison, fit DDM, DMC, DSTP, and SSP to each participant, and find that DSTP is the most frequently selected best-fitting model, but its superiority varies more across datasets than across tasks. Exploratory analyses show the 22 parameters cluster into four latent dimensions; the Inhibitory Process factor, of greatest theoretical interest in cognitive control, is unstable. Achieving cross-dataset generality of conflict diffusion models remains a major challenge.

title: Depression symptom network reorganization under internet-based emotion regulation intervention: Evidence from a large real-world cohort
description: Depression can be conceptualized as a network of interacting symptoms. Although internet-based interventions are widely used, their associations with changes in symptom network structure remain unclear. Here, in a real-world observational cohort of 26,643 adults completing an internet-based emotion regulation intervention, we examined pre–post differences in depressive symptom network structure, global connectedness, and symptom centrality, stratified by reduction status. Analyses indicated that the two core depressive symptoms (i.e., depressed mood and anhedonia) showed reduced centrality after the intervention, whereas several non-core symptoms either increased or remained unchanged. The “symptom reduction” and “symptom non-reduction” subgroups showed largely comparable network characteristics at baseline. After the intervention, the “symptom reduction” subgroup displayed lower global network strength, a reorganized network topology, and reduced centrality of the core symptoms, whereas the “symptom non-reduction” subgroup showed no significant network alteration. Further analyses using residualized symptom change scores showed a similar pattern: among individuals with comparable baseline depressive symptom severity, those with better-than-expected outcomes showed lower post-intervention network connectivity than those with poorer-than-expected outcomes. Clinically anchored improvement analyses further indicated that reduced centrality of depressed mood was observed across alternative definitions of improvement. Although causal inference is precluded by the observational design, this study provides large-scale descriptive real-world evidence on how depressive symptom networks change alongside symptom reduction during routine use of a digital intervention.

title: Recovery order in adaptive systems is set by dependency structure
description: Adaptive systems recover their capacities in reproducible orders. Predicting it has meant fitting a dynamical model to each system and reading the order off its trajectories, an output of the fit, not of structure. Here we show that recovery order follows from dependency structure: which capacities must be in place before which others recover. From four axioms we prove that where prerequisite gates vanish at baseline no capacity begins to recover before its prerequisites, whatever the rate constants, and that under a common deficit-closing rule with rates non-increasing along dependencies the admissible orders are exactly the linear extensions of the graph: a chain gives a unique sequence, a branch a partial order. We map where steep heterogeneity adds further orders. The graph is an input, realized in probabilistic models as identifiability structure. We instantiate it in catatonia, post-injury motor recovery and curriculum learning, the last without a probabilistic model.

title: The Saito Loop, a computational theory of hierarchical recovery in catatonia
description: Clinical observation identified a reproducible recovery hierarchy in catatonia, the Saito Loop (πs → β → πm → πv_fast → πv_slow), but not why recovery should follow any fixed order. We ask whether the order follows from an active-inference architecture without being supplied. The five computational quantities follow a priori from their computational roles; structural identifiability analysis then reconstructs their prerequisite relations as a directed acyclic graph. Because the graph is a chain, its topological ordering is unique and identical to the Saito Loop: the order is a structural consequence of the dependency relations, not a fitted sequence, and the complete ordering is never supplied. All uniqueness claims hold within an explicitly specified model class, and whether the structural order is realized in recovery time is a separate, falsifiable dynamical question. The clinically observed recovery hierarchy therefore becomes a constrained computational consequence rather than an empirical regularity.

title: Which Comes First: Ideology, or Moral Values? Panel evidence from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
description: Recent work has called into question the longstanding intuition that differences in political orientation are attributable to differences in moral values; instead, people may change their reported values to justify their political preferences. To identify which most plausibly causes which, we conducted a three-wave panel study, using quotas to approximate a demographically representative initial sample of U.S. adults and measuring values in four different ways, with each measure grounded in a distinct theoretical framework. We found that: 1) Ideology and partisanship consistently showed greater cross-wave stability than values. 2) Within-subject wave-to-wave shifts in political orientation and values were rarely and weakly related in either direction. Between-subjects analyses replicated existing work: conservatives and liberals tended to value different things. But during these months, respondents did not tend to become more conservative or liberal depending on what they valued, or to come to value anything more or less because of their ideology.

title: Is fashion just a fashion? Or does it have an evolutionary basis?
description: Female models presented in advertising, entertainment, and fashion shows are much slimmer on average than the general population. The fashion industry has been criticized for advertising a body type that would influence the self perception of young women, leading to eating disorders and concomitant health risks. Given the intense criticism one would expect a corresponding change in publication policies that would mitigate these negative effects. But a recent study that analyzed 25 years of published fashion records found no improvement. The present paper suggests an evolutionary explanation for why consumers prefer the unrealistic body type.

title: Stimulated recall protocols: Field-specific guidelines for second language acquisition and bilingualism research
description: Stimulated recall protocols are one of the most popular methods in second language acquisition and bilingualism research to investigate language learners’ internal thought processes when using second languages. Although methodological handbooks are available for learning how to set up a stimulated recall study, there is little empirically driven guidance on best practices for reporting variables central to the method. To develop field-specific reporting guidelines, this systematic review analyzed articles that used stimulated recall to elicit introspective reports in sixteen Q1 journals in applied linguistics between 2000 and 2024. After screening, 171 studies were analyzed for 62 variables inherent to this practice. Findings showed that some details were well-reported, but others critical for stimulated recalls, such as the use of instructions or the L2 proficiency of participants, were reported infrequently. The review concludes with empirically derived reporting guidelines derived from the literature to support authors, editors, and peer reviewers.

title: Pilot Study of Combined tDCS and Cognitive Training Intervention for Suicide Risk with Ecological Momentary Assessment: Feasibility and Acceptability in Psychiatric Inpatient Veterans
description:
Objective: This pilot study examined the feasibility and acceptability of an impulsivity-targeted neuromodulation intervention and high-density ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in high-risk veterans with suicidal thoughts and behaviors following discharge from acute inpatient psychiatric care.
Method: Fourteen adult veterans receiving acute psychiatric care screened for suicide risk were recruited to the study and completed a baseline assessment, 10 sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) paired with cognitive training, one month of EMA surveys (2-3x per day) post-discharge, and questionnaires and cognitive tasks one- and two-months following the last intervention received.
Results: Study feasibility was supported by a 21% enrollment rate, 56% intervention adherence, and no reported difficulties tolerating the intervention. Adherence to EMA surveys was high (77%) among participants who completed the EMA protocol, with the highest adherence in the first week followed by a reduction in subsequent weeks.
Conclusions: This study demonstrated that neuromodulation and cognitive training interventions and high-density EMA designs are generally feasible and acceptable among veterans at high risk of suicide following acute psychiatric care. Recommendations for increasing feasibility and adherence to such interventions and suicide risk safety procedures for intensive EMA protocols with high-risk veterans are discussed.

title: Pupil size dynamics predict momentary changes in self-reported arousal
description: Subjective arousal, or feelings of activation and alertness, can dynamically modulate affect, behavior, and cognition. Momentary changes in subjective arousal have typically been assessed with self-report in humans, which may alter those very feelings. Although researchers have traditionally used pupil size as a physiological index of arousal, links between pupil dynamics and momentary changes in subjective arousal remain unclear. Here, we combined continuous pupillometry with repeated self-report probes of changing arousal as individuals engaged in a modified Monetary Incentive Delay task. Across Virtual Reality (N = 28; 12 females, 16 males) and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (N = 27; 15 females, 12 males) studies, tonic and phasic pupil measures jointly predicted subsequent self-reported arousal beyond stated incentive value and at a temporal lag of approximately 1.5–3.5 seconds. Neural activity associated with pupil dynamics further predicted pupil size, self-reported arousal, and behavioral motivation in held-out data. Together, these convergent findings establish pupil size as a temporally-precise marker of momentary fluctuations in self-reported arousal.

title: Imagination boosts strategy learning
description: Imagination is thought to boost exploration and problem solving by simulating states that have not been directly experienced as a means of reasoning through future plans. Here we tested this idea in the context of an impartial combinatorial game with a ground truth optional strategy. Adopting a stumbler-strategist reinforcement learning architecture, we showed how imagination can boost optimal strategy learning over memory replay. These model predictions were validated experimentally in humans (N=255) using an intervention design where participants were tasked with either imagining unplayed scenarios, reviewing prior games, or engaging in a simple visual attention task (control). These convergent results show how imagination uniquely boosts strategy learning in partially explored tasks.

title: FLM UNGOAL: A Factor-Label Method for Removing Semantic Distractors in Health Behavior Change
description:
Health behavior change frequently fails despite genuine patient motivation and adequate health literacy. This article presents a proof-of-concept single-subject case study (N=1) investigating the FLM UNGOAL framework—a novel cognitive-identity restructuring protocol using the Factor-Label Method (dimensional analysis) to systematically remove ungoal distractors (maladaptive Past Self cognitions in QIII) and transfer identity to the Future I (QI) via a diagonal conversion vector through a 4-region trigonometric spatial architecture.
Participant: A 42-year-old bilingual Persian-Iranian male (native Persian, fluent German) with Type 2 Diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) and poor treatment adherence. Procedure: Following a 7-day baseline, the participant engaged in 6 sessions (90 min each) over 6 weeks using the FLM UNGOAL Board and protocol. Measures: Tri-Circle Overlap Index (TCOI), Goal Proximity Index (GPI), Conversion Factor (CF), daily practice logs. Results: TCOI improved from 0.18 (baseline, high Past Self identification) to 3.00 (post-intervention, Future I dominant) to 5.67 (maintenance). GPI increased from 15% to 85%. CF increased from N/A to 5.7. HbA1c improved from 8.2% to 7.0% at 3-month follow-up. Qualitative reports confirmed reduced cognitive friction and sustained identity transfer.
The framework integrates embodied cognition (Lakoff & Johnson, 1999), the Tri-Circle Temporal Self Model (Markus & Nurius, 1986; Higgins, 1987), industrial design principles via the FLM UNGOAL Board, complex systems theory, and Measurement-Based Care principles (Fortney et al., 2017). The 4-region trigonometric circle maps valence (Y-axis: Positive/Negative) and temporality (X-axis: Future/Past) with Cartesian independence—Fear is precisely localized to QIV (Future + Negative) and deliberately bypassed by the diagonal conversion vector. title: Addiction as a Chronic Brain Disease: A Narrative Review of the Neurobiological Evidence
description:
Addiction has traditionally been explained in moral terms, as a failure of discipline repeated one
too many times. Three decades of neuroscience research complicate that story considerably.
Repeated exposure to alcohol and other drugs changes how the brain's reward circuitry responds
to everyday experience, weakens the prefrontal systems responsible for planning and impulse
control, and leaves behind changes to stress and memory circuits that can persist long after drug
use has stopped. This narrative review draws on major research syntheses, including work by
Volkow, Koob, and colleagues and Heilig and colleagues' 2021 reassessment of the brain disease
model, to lay out the neurobiological case for classifying addiction as a chronic brain disease. It
also takes seriously the strongest published objections to that framing, including Sally Satel and
Scott Lilienfeld's argument that a heavily biological account can understate the role of choice and
context, Gene Heyman's evidence on unassisted recovery, and experimental work showing that a
disease-focused message can reduce people's stated intent to seek treatment. The review
concludes that the neurobiological evidence is substantial enough to support the disease
classification, but that the classification works best when paired with, rather than substituted for,
personal responsibility and psychosocial treatment. It closes with a discussion of clinical and
1 policy implications and the limits of a narrative review built on a curated set of sources rather
than a systematic literature search.

title: Bilingual experience predicts language skills, but not reading skills, in a low-literacy and multilingual context
description: Children throughout the world attend school and learn to read in a language of instruction (LoI) other than the language(s) they speak at home, which is one factor contributing to poor reading outcomes. Understanding reading development in multilingual, Majority World contexts is important for improving reading skills globally. In a linguistically diverse sample of children in rural Côte d’Ivoire, we examined how home language experience (monolingual, regional bilingual [two Ivorian languages], French bilingual [French + Ivorian language], French multilingual [French + two Ivorian languages]) relates to children’s (N = 1335) language and reading skills. Bilingual children (French and regional) outperformed monolingual children on French language tasks, suggesting bilingual experience benefits language skills regardless of whether it includes the LoI (French). However, this language advantage did not extend to reading; there were no differences in reading scores between groups and all children leveraged phonological awareness for reading regardless of their home language experience. The findings suggest that bilingual/multilingual education programs, and reading instruction that strengthens language skills, may support reading outcomes in multilingual, Majority World contexts.

title: Welcome to the Jangle (Fallacy): The Case of Statistics and Mathematics Anxieties
description:
Background: Statistics-related anxiety is a common barrier to learning in higher education, particularly for psychology and other non-specialist students. High prevalence rates are concerning because statistical literacy is integral to academic success, employability, and informed citizenship. Clarifying the nature of statistics anxiety is central to understanding it, yet it remains unclear whether statistics anxiety is genuinely distinct from mathematics anxiety or simply another manifestation of the same construct.

Aims: We examined the degree of overlap (jangle fallacy) between the Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS) and the Revised Mathematics Anxiety Rating Scale (R-MARS).

Samples: Two cohorts of UK undergraduate psychology students participated: Study 1 (n = 489) and Study 2 (n = 245).

Methods: Each study combined a cross-sectional survey with a between-participants experiment. Surveys included the STARS, R-MARS, parallel forms to control for scale content, and measures of trait and state anxiety. In the experiment, participants were randomly assigned to complete either a statistics or mathematics multiple-choice test, with state anxiety measured before and after.

Results:
Results pointed to overlap across all analyses and samples. Scales were highly correlated, items did not separate into distinct domains, individuals rarely reported one without the other, and state anxiety increased similarly across test types.

Conclusions:
Findings show that statistics anxiety, as measured by the STARS, is not distinct from mathematics anxiety, as measured by the R-MARS. Recognising statistics anxiety as part of the broader mathematics anxiety construct can streamline measurement, clarify theory, and support more effective interventions for reducing quantitative anxieties in education.

title: The Behavioural Effects of Cash-Out Availability in a Naturalistic Betting Task: Results of a Randomised Experiment
description:
Introduction: People place larger bets on risky events when they can cash-out before the bet concludes. This study experimentally investigates how cash-out availability impacts wider betting behaviour in a simulated betting task and whether risk of gambling problems moderates observed effects.
Method: An incentivised, between-participants online experiment (n=377; 70.8% males, 28.6% females; Mage = 39.9), where participants could place bets on horse races via a simulated bookmaker’s website. Participants were randomly assigned to either have the option of cashing-out their bets or not. We examined choices to engage with the gambling task, stake sizes and implied win probabilities of placed bets, and measured risk of gambling problems by administering the PGSI.
Results: The cash-out group was more likely to choose the gambling task over a distractor game (χ²(1, N=377)=4.59, p=0.032) and engaged with the gambling task for longer than the no-cash-out group (β=0.61, SE=0.23, p=0.0077). The cash-out group also made larger bets (W=19761.5, p=0.021), though this finding was more nuanced. There was no effect of cash-out availability on the average odds of placed bets (W=10635.5, p=0.67). No significant interactions between cash-out availability and PGSI were observed for either the implied win probability of placed bets (β<0.01, SE<0.01, p=0.44) or stake size (β=-0.02, SE=0.02, p=0.15), though a subgroup analysis revealed groupwise differences in stake size within a low-PGSI (W=6909.5, p=0.0076, n=260) subgroup. No such difference was found in the high-PGSI subgroup (W=1699.5, p=0.89, n=117).
Conclusion: The provision of cash-out options in betting products results in significant changes in betting behaviour, which could potentially lead to increased risk of gambling harms.

title: How we see relations: the case of containment and support
description: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography (EEG) on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens (“in” or “on”) but rather as objects’ properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning.

title: Impaired Interoception as a Pathway from Binge-Eating Severity to Self-Regulatory Dysfunction and Hedonic Food Responsiveness
description: Binge eating has been linked to alterations in interoceptive awareness, self-regulation, and hedonic responsiveness to food, yet the mechanisms connecting these domains remain incompletely understood. The present study examined differences in interoceptive awareness, executive functioning, and hedonic responsiveness to food across levels of binge-eating severity in a community sample of adults. Participants completed self-report measures assessing multidimensional interoceptive awareness, executive functioning, and food reward sensitivity, as well as a battery of neuropsychological tasks evaluating inhibition, cognitive flexibility, and decision-making. Structural equation modeling was used to compare five theoretically grounded alternative models describing the relationships among these constructs. Individuals with higher binge-eating severity showed greater hedonic responsiveness to food cues, higher levels of negative urgency, reduced perseverance, and greater self-reported executive difficulties, alongside lower interoceptive awareness across several dimensions. In contrast, performance-based neuropsychological tasks did not reliably differentiate binge-eating severity groups. Binge-eating severity was associated with hedonic food responsiveness both directly and indirectly through reduced interoceptive awareness and self-regulatory dysfunction. These findings suggest that binge-eating severity may be more strongly related to subjective and experiential aspects of self-regulation and bodily awareness than to deficits detected through classical neuropsychological tasks and point to interoceptive awareness as a transdiagnostic mechanism through which binge-eating severity may amplify hedonic food responsiveness via self-regulatory dysfunction.
